analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to raise oil prices within 30 days of a war declaration, U.S. military action, or a major oil spill.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, drew only 2 cosponsors, and died there when the 101st Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it a federal crime, punishable by a fine or up to three years in prison, to raise the price of crude oil, gasoline, heating fuel, diesel, propane, or other petroleum products within 30 days of a declaration of war, the sending of U.S. forces into hostilities, or a federal agency being notified of an oil discharge. A price increase would still be legal if the seller could show it only covered the seller's actual higher cost. It also required the President or the relevant federal agency to publish notice of these triggering events in the Federal Register so sellers and the public would know the rule was in effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who buy gasoline, home heating oil, diesel, and propane. The bill targeted the pattern — visible after the 1990 Iraqi invasion of Kuwait sent crude prices soaring — of fuel prices jumping within days of a crisis or disaster, often faster and further than the seller's own costs rose. By making unjustified crisis-period increases a crime rather than merely a civil antitrust matter, it would have given families a direct price shield precisely when a war or spill was already squeezing their budgets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers of gasoline and heating fuel

how_it_helps.text: It would have imposed a fine, up to three years' imprisonment, or both, on anyone raising crude oil or refined petroleum product prices within 30 days of a declaration of war, the introduction of U.S. forces into hostilities, or a federal agency's notification of an oil discharge — unless the increase was justified by the seller's actual cost.

The covered products include gasoline, kerosene, distillates such as number 2 fuel oil, propane and butane (LPG), lubricating oils, and diesel fuel — the fuels households and small businesses burn for cars, homes, and equipment.

It required the President, or the federal agency notified of an oil discharge, to publish notice in the Federal Register as soon as possible, so both sellers and consumers would have official notice that the crisis pricing rule was in effect.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, wholesalers, and fuel retailers, who would face federal criminal liability — fines or up to three years' imprisonment — for crisis-period price increases they could not tie to their own actual costs. The federal government would also bear the cost of publishing the Federal Register notices.

drawbacks.text: The 'actual cost' exception would be hard to apply: a seller buying crude on the world market would have to prove each price increase was justified by its real input costs, inviting litigation and enforcement disputes over what counts as actual cost in a fast-moving market.

The freeze applies only in the 30 days after a declaration of war, the introduction of U.S. forces into hostilities, or a federal oil-discharge notification — a narrow trigger that leaves ordinary supply disruptions and market swings untouched, and an honest supporter would concede the protection is limited to those windows.

Economists generally argue that price-gouging bans can discourage hoarding-preventing stock building and cause shortages, because holding prices down during a spike removes the signal that draws extra supply in — a real cost an honest supporter of this bill would have to weigh against the consumer protection.
Criminal penalties (up to three years) for ordinary commercial pricing decisions are a heavy tool; the bill provided no civil penalty alternative for smaller or first-time violations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it would have directly protected household fuel budgets during exactly the moments — a war, a military action, a major spill — when fuel prices historically spike fastest, and the actual-cost exception kept legitimate price pass-through legal. The costs are that the protection covers only a 30-day window after narrow triggering events, that proving 'actual cost' would be contentious, and that criminal penalties for pricing decisions are blunt instruments that economists worry could worsen shortages. On balance a modest, defensible consumer protection rather than a sweeping price-control regime — and it was never given the chance to be tested, debated, or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in early January 1991.

narrative.text: Representative Dennis Hertel introduced the bill on September 17, 1990, during the Gulf crisis that had begun with Iraq's invasion of Kuwait the previous month, when world crude prices roughly doubled and U.S. gasoline prices spiked.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Judiciary the same day and received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote is recorded in its action history.
It attracted only 2 cosponsors, both House Democrats, in the roughly three and a half months before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel sellers — and the major oil companies profiting from crisis-period price spikes — were better off because the bill never advanced; consumers got no protection against wartime or spill-related fuel price increases.

for.name: Dennis M. Hertel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

for.name: 2 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; Representative Michael McNulty was one of the two.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Jack Brooks (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and petroleum industry
against.what_they_did: The bill would have exposed producers, refiners, and fuel sellers to criminal penalties for crisis-period price increases; no support for the measure is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough to produce a vote; its only support came from 3 House Democrats (the sponsor and 2 cosponsors), and no Republican or Democratic leadership action for or against it appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have made it a crime, punishable by fine or up to three years in prison, for them to raise crude or refined product prices within 30 days of a war declaration, U.S. forces entering hostilities, or a notified oil discharge unless the increase matched their actual costs. It directly targeted the industry's ability to profit from crisis-driven price spikes.

industries.industry: Fuel wholesalers and retailers (gasoline, heating oil, diesel, propane)
industries.note: Sellers of the covered refined products faced the same criminal exposure for crisis-window markups not justified by actual cost. Their interest in keeping emergency-period pricing unrestricted ran against household fuel budgets.

The bill added a paperwork duty: the President or the relevant agency would have to publish notice of the triggering event, including the full text of the penalty provision, in the Federal Register as soon as possible. A minor administrative burden in service of consumer notice.
